sections.body:
The theory of war is the name for a body of ideas about how conflict works. It is not a manual of fighting and it is not a set of rules for winning. It is the accumulated thinking of officers and writers who studied past campaigns and tried to write down what they saw. The best-known of them is Carl von Clausewitz, a Prussian officer whose book On War was published in 1832, after his death.

The ideas are old, but the vocabulary is alive. News agencies, ministry briefings, staff papers, think-tank reports and study books all use it: strategy, operational, attrition, escalation, deterrence, decisive point. A reader who meets these words without knowing them guesses from the words around them, and the guess is often wrong. The offensive failed and the offensive was called off are not the same statement, and only the vocabulary tells them apart.

This article is about that vocabulary and the reasoning behind it, as history and analysis. It explains what the words mean, where they come from and how they are used in English. It does not teach anyone to fight, and it does not describe how any conflict should be won.
examples: The paper is about the theory of war, not about the conduct of the war.
The report uses the vocabulary of the theory of war: objective, decisive point, lines of communication.
Learning the theory of war means learning the English of security writing.
sections.heading: The theory of war: a set of ideas, not a manual

terms.example: The book is called a theory of war because it explains how conflict works, not how to fight.
terms.gloss: A body of ideas about how conflict works, built from the study of past campaigns rather than from rules of fighting.

sections.body:
Clausewitz gave the field its central sentence in On War, published in 1832: "War is merely the continuation of policy by other means." Read it slowly. War is a continuation, so it is not a separate world. It is the same business as politics — a state managing its relations and its disputes — carried on with force instead of with argument.

That sentence explains why a war has a political purpose that can be read off the wire: the fighting is aimed at a result, and the result is a political one. It also explains why the end of a war is usually written in a treaty. The treaty is where the politics is settled and the weapons are put down.

The sentence is often misread, so it is worth being exact about what it does not say. It does not say that war is only politics: force changes the situation, and a state that ignores the military facts is reasoning about a country that does not exist. It does not say that war is random: for Clausewitz war is a political act, and it can be studied like one. It does not say that every war has a just cause: the word policy means the aims of the state, whatever those aims are. And it does not say that war is the best way to settle a dispute. It says what war is when it happens, not that it should happen.

For a reader of briefs and news, the sentence is a check. When a report calls a conflict a continuation of politics, it is claiming that there is an aim behind the fighting, and it is inviting you to ask what that aim is and who holds it. The July Crisis of 1914 is the classic case. The fighting of that summer grew out of a chain of decisions taken by governments in the weeks after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in June 1914. Each side answered a political question, and the answers together produced a general war.
examples: The war was the continuation of the politics; the settlement had to match it.
Clausewitz did not say that war is only politics; he said it is politics with force added.
Read the sentence as a question: what political aim does this fighting serve?
sections.heading: War as the continuation of politics by other means

terms.example: Clausewitz wrote that war is the continuation of politics by other means.
terms.gloss: The Prussian officer (1780-1831) who wrote On War, the book that gave the field its central sentence.

terms.example: The war had a political purpose, so the settlement had to satisfy the politics.
terms.gloss: The business of running a state and its relations with other states; in the theory of war, the purpose that fighting is meant to serve.

sections.body:
Conflict is read on a ladder. At the top is politics: what the state wants. Under it is strategy: how the aim is pursued, with which means, over what time. Under strategy is operations: the campaign as it is carried out, across the front, week by week. Under operations is tactics: the local action, one fight, one unit, one afternoon. A campaign is the chain of connected actions that runs from the first move to the decision that closes it.

The levels are not a rank. A decision at one level constrains the levels below it, and the levels below report back with facts the level above did not have. A tactical success that changes nothing at the strategic level is not a success. A strategic aim that no tactics can deliver is not an aim. That is why a good brief states the level it is speaking about, and why a reader should ask: is this sentence about the policy, the strategy, the operations or the fight?

One word needs care at the top. Strategy at the level of a whole state is often called grand strategy: the way a country uses its power over years to reach a political aim. Deterrence, alliance and economic pressure are usual tools of grand strategy, and the terms recur in English-language security writing.
examples: The sentence is about strategy; the paragraph under it is about tactics.
A campaign is the chain of actions from the first move to the decision.
Grand strategy links the military means to the political aim.
sections.heading: Strategy, operations, tactics: the ladder from politics to the fight

terms.example: The strategy of the campaign was to hold the coast and wait.
terms.gloss: The way a conflict is linked to its political purpose: what is wanted, with what means, over what time.

terms.example: The operations ran out of fuel before the plan reached its objective.
terms.gloss: The level between strategy and tactics: the way a whole campaign is carried out, across a front, week by week.

terms.example: The report describes tactics when it explains how the advance was carried out.
terms.gloss: The level of the local action: how a unit is used in one fight and how it is moved on the field.

terms.example: The campaign lasted six weeks and ended at the river.
terms.gloss: A series of connected actions with one objective, from the first move to the decision that closes it.

terms.example: Containment was the grand strategy, and deterrence was one of its tools.
terms.gloss: Strategy at the level of a whole state: how a country uses its power over years to reach a political aim.

sections.body:
The classical theory gives a short list of elements that every plan needs. The list has been used in English for two centuries, and it is the fastest way to read a brief that describes an operation without naming these things. Ask for the five, in this order, and the shape of the plan appears.

The order matters. The objective comes first, because everything else is chosen to serve it. The lines of approach follow, because they decide how the objective can be reached at all. The decisive point comes next: the place where the outcome is settled. The reserves and the lines of communication come last, because they are what the plan needs when the first effort has not worked.
examples: The brief names the objective but not the decisive point.
No reserve was kept, so the plan had nothing left for the second week.
The lines of communication ran through one bridge.
sections.heading: The five elements of a campaign: a checklist for reading a brief
steps: Name the objective: the result the plan wants, written so that someone can say whether it has been reached.
Find the lines of approach: the directions from which the attack may come and the ground they must cross.
Locate the decisive point: the place or the moment where the outcome of the whole action is settled.
Check the reserves: the means held back for the moment when the situation turns, so the plan is not spent at the first contact.
Trace the lines of communication: the routes along which orders, reports and supplies reach the fighting units.

terms.example: The brief states the objective in one line: the river crossing.
terms.gloss: The result a plan aims at, written so that it can be judged done or not done.

terms.example: The lines of approach were limited by the marsh.
terms.gloss: The directions from which an attack may come, and the ground they must cross.

terms.example: The decisive point was the bridge, and the plan said so.
terms.gloss: The place or the moment where the outcome of the whole action is settled; the effort is concentrated there.

terms.example: The plan kept one reserve for the second week.
terms.gloss: Means held back from the first effort and kept for the moment the situation turns.

terms.example: The lines of communication were cut by the flood.
terms.gloss: The routes along which orders, reports and supplies travel to the fighting units.

sections.body:
Friction is the constant distance between what a plan says and what happens. It is not bad luck. It is the ordinary condition of acting on incomplete information, through tired people, over distance, in bad weather, with supplies that arrive late. Small difficulties multiply: a delay of a day here, a wrong report there, an engine that fails, and the plan has changed without anybody deciding to change it.

Clausewitz used the image of a fog to describe the second half of the problem. In war the fog is thick: the commander sees fragments — a report, a rumour, a column on the road — and has to act on a picture that is always incomplete and sometimes false. The fog is the uncertainty of information, not the weather. He used the image to say something more general: nobody holds the whole field, so a plan must be made to survive being wrong about part of it.

That is why the theory treats friction as something a plan absorbs, not something to be wished away. Reserves exist for it. A margin of time exists for it. A clear objective exists for it, because the aim is the one part of a plan that should not move when the fog thickens. A reader who finds that a plan has no reserve and no margin should read it as a plan that assumes perfect information.
examples: The plan met friction: the bridge was down and the orders were late.
In the fog of war every report is three days old.
A plan with no reserve assumes that nothing will go wrong.
sections.heading: Friction: why the plan meets the fog

terms.example: Every plan met friction: the weather, the delay, the wrong order.
terms.gloss: The constant gap between what a plan says and what happens on the ground.

terms.example: In the fog of war the commander acted on a report three days old.
terms.gloss: The state of not knowing: incomplete reports, false information and the general uncertainty of events.

sections.body:
Escalation is the widening of a conflict. A limited exchange becomes a larger one: more parties are drawn in, the scale of the fighting rises, or the aims grow until the dispute is no longer the one that started. Analysts describe escalation as a ladder, because each step is smaller than the next and each step is meant to be readable by the other side. Staying low on the ladder keeps the other side's steps small too.

Escalation can be deliberate or accidental. A government may climb the ladder on purpose, to raise the price of the other side's action. It can also climb it by accident, when a move meant to look small is read as large and the reply is made to look small in turn. The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 is the best-known case of both. The crisis moved up the ladder step by step, and it came down again because both sides read the steps of the other and stopped.

Deterrence is the effort to prevent an action, not to win an argument. It works by making the cost of the action higher than the gain, so that the other side chooses not to act. For deterrence to hold, the other side must believe two things: that the capability exists, and that the will to use it exists. Deterrence failure is the case where the opponent acts anyway — either because the threat was not believed, or because it was believed and the cost was accepted. The second case is not a mistake; it is a calculation.

Deterrence is not the same as a bluff. A bluff is a threat made without the means or the intention to carry it out. Deterrence is backed by real capability and a real intention. The word to keep in mind is credibility: whether the other side believes you will do what you said. The same careful reading applies to asymmetric conflict, where the two sides are not alike. Their resources, organisation and methods differ greatly, and the analysis turns on where the difference lies rather than on which side is larger.
examples: The crisis climbed three rungs of the escalation ladder in a week.
The threat was not believed, so the action went ahead.
An empty threat is a bluff; a threat backed by capability and will is deterrence.
sections.heading: Escalation and deterrence: how a conflict grows, and how it is meant not to

terms.example: The escalation was deliberate, and every step was announced.
terms.gloss: The widening of a conflict: more parties, a larger scale, or a new aim.

terms.example: Analysts place the crisis three rungs up the escalation ladder.
terms.gloss: The ladder of steps a conflict can climb, from a limited incident up to a general war.

terms.example: Deterrence holds only if the opponent believes both the ability and the will.
terms.gloss: The effort to prevent an opponent's action by making the cost of it too high.

terms.example: Deterrence failure means the action went ahead anyway.
terms.gloss: The case where the opponent acts anyway: the threat was not believed, or it was believed and the cost was accepted.

terms.example: A threat made without the means to carry it out is a bluff, and it costs nothing to make.
terms.gloss: A threat that is made without the means or the intention to carry it out.

terms.example: The article calls it an asymmetric conflict and says where the difference lies.
terms.gloss: A conflict between opponents whose resources, organisation and methods differ greatly.

sections.body:
The words below are the ones that meet the reader in briefs, news reports and study books. The middle column gives the short meaning; the third column gives a sentence of the kind the word appears in.

Words that the article has already defined keep the same meaning here. The table is a check on the vocabulary of a document, not a summary of the article.
examples: The table is a quick check: does the brief use these words in this sense?
Read the word inside its sentence; the vocabulary changes the meaning of the report.
sections.heading: The vocabulary of the field

rows: Strategy
How the conflict is linked to its political purpose.
The strategy was to hold the coast and wait.
Tactics
How a local action is fought, one unit at a time.
The tactics changed once the ammunition ran low.
Deterrence
Preventing an action by making its cost too high.
Deterrence depends on the other side believing it.
Escalation
The widening of a conflict in scale, parties or aims.
The escalation widened the conflict in three steps.
Attrition
Wearing the opponent down by continued cost.
Attrition, not one battle, decided the campaign.
Front
The line where the two sides meet.
The front held for three months.
Offensive
The side that attacks, and the direction of the action.
The offensive stopped when the supplies ran out.
Defensive
The side that receives the attack and holds ground.
A defensive plan is judged by the ground it gives up.
Logistics
Moving and supplying the fighting.
The report says the problem was logistics.
Morale
The spirit and the confidence of a force.
Morale fell as the convoy did not arrive.
Decisive point
Where the outcome of the whole action is settled.
The decisive point was the river crossing.
Friction
The gap between the plan and what happens.
Every plan met friction.

terms.example: Attrition decided the campaign; no single battle did.
terms.gloss: The wearing down of the opponent by continued cost, rather than by one decisive stroke.

terms.example: The front held for three months while both sides rebuilt.
terms.gloss: The line where the two sides stand against each other, and the whole stretch of fighting behind it.

terms.example: The offensive stopped when the supplies ran out.
terms.gloss: The side that attacks; in the phrase the offensive, the direction of the action.

terms.example: A defensive plan is judged by the ground it gives up.
terms.gloss: The side that receives the attack and holds ground; the opposite of the offensive.

terms.example: The report says the problem was logistics, not the fighting.
terms.gloss: The work of moving and supplying the fighting: food, fuel, ammunition, vehicles and spares.

terms.example: Morale fell as the third convoy did not arrive.
terms.gloss: The spirit and the confidence of a force; the strength it holds when things go badly.

sections.body:
The sentences below are the ones a reader of briefs and reports meets most often, written in the plainest form.

Use them to name what a document says, and to ask for what it leaves out.
examples: The brief does not name a decisive point.
The escalation was deliberate.
The deterrence failed on the first sign.
The plan kept one reserve for the second week.
sections.heading: Sentences for the brief and the report

item.summary: Security briefs, news reports and study books all use the words of the theory of war. After reading this you can explain Clausewitz's central sentence, tell strategy from operations and tactics, name the five classical elements of a campaign, say what friction and escalation mean, and use the vocabulary of deterrence, attrition and morale in a sentence of your own.
item.title: The Theory of War: Strategy, Tactics and the Politics Behind It
